description: Hi! I'm a Computer Science student at the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU), and I'm also a pixel artist.
summary:
Stellar Pixel is an interactive pixel-art lunar base management game built in Unity WebGL that turns real space-weather data into playable survival decisions. Players command a 4-astronaut lunar outpost over a 30-day mission, building and wiring power, water, food, and oxygen grids while keeping cumulative radiation exposure below NASA’s 250 mSv safety limit.

Using open datasets from NASA DONKI, Curiosity RAD, LRO CRaTER, and Apollo archives, the game simulates historical solar flares and geomagnetic storms such as the August 1972 Superstorm and the May 2024 G5 storm. When alerts arrive, players must manage resource trade-offs such as spending water and power on emergency shielding or upgrading the Habitat against higher daily upkeep. By turning real space radiation and life-support data into a clear browser game, Stellar Pixel helps students and the public understand the survival challenges astronauts face on the Moon.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Stellar Pixel is a 2D pixel-art lunar base management game that runs directly in the browser. You manage a 4-astronaut outpost over a 30-day mission, keeping life support running while dealing with real space weather.

  • Building & Wiring Grids: You earn Lunar Credits by completing missions and surviving events, then spend them in the Shop ([T]) to place 7 different modules: Solar Panels, Water Generators, Greenhouses, Oxygen Generators, Power Storage, and Water Tanks. To automate resource collection and expand your reserves, you press [C] to drag power cables and water pipes between generators and storage tanks.
  • Daily Life Support: Every lunar day, the central Habitat ([H]) consumes Energy, Water, Food, and Oxygen based on your crew size. You can upgrade the Habitat across 5 levels to raise radiation protection (from 0% up to 70%) and boost production, though higher levels also increase daily energy and water upkeep.
  • Radiation & Solar Storms: A 30-day dosimeter on the top HUD tracks the crew's cumulative radiation against NASA's 250 mSv limit, starting from the Moon's natural 1.37 mSv/day background radiation. When a solar flare or coronal mass ejection is detected, you get a short warning window to stock up on water and power before deciding how to respond—such as pumping water into hydrogen-rich wall shields that block up to 85% of incoming solar protons.


How We Used NASA & Space Agency Open Data

We used open spaceflight datasets to set the numbers, hazards, and survival mechanics in the game:

  1. NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): Used to model real solar flares and coronal mass ejections, including the September 2017 X9.3 Solar Flare and the May 2024 G5 Geomagnetic Storm.
  2. NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) CRaTER: Used for the Moon's baseline radiation rate of 1.37 mSv/day from galactic cosmic rays.
  3. NASA Curiosity RAD & Apollo Records: Used to scale Solar Particle Event radiation spikes, including the August 1972 Solar Superstorm (350+ mSv unshielded) that happened between Apollo 16 and Apollo 17.
  4. NASA ECLSS & Artemis Base Camp Concepts: Used to balance daily crew water, oxygen, food, and power consumption, showing why water is both a daily necessity and a primary radiation shield on the Moon.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Making Radiation Visible: Space radiation numbers like millisieverts (mSv) and solar proton events are hard to picture from a textbook. Turning them into a resource-management problem helps players see how quickly exposure adds up without an atmosphere or magnetic field.
  • Showing Real Engineering Trade-Offs: There is no single upgrade that solves everything. Raising Habitat shielding costs more power and water every day, and using water reserves to block solar storms leaves less water for oxygen production and crops.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Engine & Code: Unity and C#.
  • Art: Aseprite (all sprites, modules, icons, and animations drawn pixel by pixel).
  • Web: Unity WebGL, HTML5, Tailwind CSS and JavaScript.
  • Reference Data: NASA DONKI, NASA-STD-3001 radiation limits, Curiosity RAD, NASA LRO CRaTER lunar dosimetry data.
